text: A UI Policy is a record on the sys_ui_policy table, and it exists to make a form behave intelligently as someone fills it in. Think of an Incident form where selecting Category equals Hardware should reveal an Asset Tag field that's completely irrelevant for every other category. Instead of cluttering the form permanently, or hand-writing a client script, an administrator builds a UI Policy: a condition, like Category is Hardware, paired with the field behavior that condition should trigger. The policy record itself holds the table it governs, the condition, whether it's active, and an order value for when multiple policies could apply to the same form.

The real field-level work happens in a related list called UI Policy Actions. Each action names one specific field and sets exactly one of three effects: Visible, which shows or hides the field; Mandatory, which requires a value before the form can submit; or Read-only, which displays the field but blocks typing into it. A single UI Policy can carry several actions across different fields at once. Each action also has a reverse-if-false setting, almost always left on, which automatically undoes the effect the moment the condition stops being true — so the field hides itself again the instant the user changes Category away from Hardware.

What makes this genuinely useful is that it evaluates live, directly in the browser, with no save and no page refresh. The instant a user changes the Category field, the condition re-checks immediately on the client, and Asset Tag appears, disappears, becomes mandatory, or stops being mandatory in real time. This is the identical mechanism behind Catalog UI Policies from Chapter 3 — the platform-wide sys_ui_policy behavior doesn't change whether the form is an Incident, a Change Request, or a catalog item's variable set. Only the table being governed changes.

Here is the single most important limitation to carry forward: a UI Policy only controls what happens inside the browser, on that specific rendered form. It has zero effect on a record written any other way — a background script run by another admin, a scheduled Import Set pulling rows from a spreadsheet, or an external system calling a Scripted REST API directly. In every one of those paths the form never renders, so the UI Policy never evaluates, and a record can be saved with Asset Tag completely blank even though the policy insists it's mandatory whenever Category is Hardware.

That gap isn't a bug — a UI Policy was simply never designed as a data-integrity mechanism; it's a form-experience mechanism, full stop. When a rule genuinely has to hold true no matter how the record reaches the database, that calls for a different tool entirely. Next up: Data Policies, which close exactly that gap at the server level, regardless of which door the write comes through.
